author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Test Android Battery Saver impact on PS2 emulation
summary: Compare a fixed PS2 route with Battery Saver explicitly off and on, while holding charge level, temperature, brightness, renderer, and background activity constant, then document whether speed loss comes from system power policy.
heroAlt: Power-plan controls illustrating a controlled comparison between normal and restricted performance policies

blocks.text: Isolate the operating-system policy from battery percentage

Battery Saver can change CPU scheduling, background activity, display behavior, and vendor-specific performance limits. A phone that becomes slower near a particular charge level may also be warming, dimming, or entering an automatic mode. Use the same short but demanding route twice at a middle charge range: first with Battery Saver explicitly disabled, then with it explicitly enabled. Record the mode rather than assuming its icon tells the whole story.
Do not benchmark the off pass at a full cool charge and the on pass at a low warm charge. That comparison mixes power policy, temperature, voltage, and elapsed play time.
Create matched off and on conditions

items: A deterministic three-to-five-minute gameplay route with one demanding section.
Battery level kept within a narrow middle range for both passes.
Identical display brightness, refresh rate, renderer, driver, and per-game profile.
The device cooled to the same idle condition before each run.
A note of automatic Battery Saver thresholds and any vendor game mode.

blocks.text: Measure the policy as the only changed variable

items: 1. Disable automatic Battery Saver scheduling for the duration of the experiment.
2. Set Battery Saver off, cold-boot the game, and complete one cache warm-up pass.
3. Restart from the same save and record speed, frame time, audio cadence, and temperature landmarks.
4. Cool the device back to the documented starting state without charging through the test range.
5. Enable Battery Saver manually and confirm the status in Android settings.
6. Repeat the same warm-up and measured route with no emulator changes.
7. Toggle Battery Saver off once more and run a short confirmation at the heaviest landmark.
8. Record the result as device- and firmware-specific rather than a universal Android rule.

blocks.text: The final off confirmation guards against a scene change, cache event, or temperature drift masquerading as policy impact. A repeatable loss that begins immediately with Battery Saver and disappears when it is disabled supports a system-policy diagnosis. A late decline in both modes points instead toward sustained thermal behavior.
Accept the conclusion only when the mode change produces the same direction of effect under matched conditions.

items: Charge, temperature, brightness, and route are comparable.
The emulator profile and cache state remain unchanged.
The on pass shows a repeatable timing difference, not one isolated hitch.
The final off confirmation returns toward the original behavior.
Automatic thresholds and vendor game modes are documented.
Android automatically re-enables the mode at a threshold: disable scheduling and repeat.
The game route contains random load: choose a deterministic checkpoint.
The second pass starts hotter: wait for the same baseline.
A vendor performance panel changes settings too: test that layer separately.

blocks.text: Return Battery Saver scheduling and vendor game controls to their previous state, remove diagnostic overlays, and restore the accepted per-game profile. Keep the small results table with the Android build number so a future firmware change can be retested accurately.
Vendors may add policies beyond stock Android

Two devices on the same Android version can react differently because firmware selects frequencies, thermal targets, and game-mode exceptions. The procedure proves behavior for the tested device state; it does not justify forcing a high-power mode on every phone.
